fields.CreateRLSFilterID: @lookup:MJ: Row Level Security Filters.Name=MJ Forms: Respondent Gate Only, Never A Writer

_comments: The four Form Respondent grants in this file carry their RLS filter by @lookup, so a
REGENERATED metadata seed reproduces the FILTERED state instead of the exploitable one
(#39). Verified by real push, not assumed: the generated SQL emits
@CreateRLSFilterID = '7F0E0001-...' and drops that column's _Clear flag, where before this
it emitted @CreateRLSFilterID_Clear = 1 -- an explicit NULL, which is the vulnerability.
THE FILTER RECORDS THEMSELVES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT IN metadata/, and this is not an
oversight to correct. MJ grants NO role Create on 'MJ: Row Level Security Filters'
(Developer holds Read + Delete; Integration and UI hold Read), so `mj sync push` fails
outright on them -- 'Does NOT have permission to Create MJ: Row Level Security Filters'.
They are created by V202608131600 and must stay there. Adding a
metadata/row-level-security-filters/ directory does not work; it was tried.
CONSEQUENCE FOR THE REGENERATION RECIPE: the three filter records must EXIST in the
database before you push, and the teardown script deletes them (they are in its doom
list). See migrations/README.md. If they are missing the push FAILS LOUDLY -- 'Lookup
failed: No record found in MJ: Row Level Security Filters' -- which is the desired
behaviour: it cannot silently regress to an unfiltered grant.
Five further grants (Forms, Form Questions, Form Question Options, Form Pages, Form
Styles) were removed from this file and are DELETEd by that same migration: no anonymous
code path ever read them, because the published version's DefinitionSnapshot already
carries the whole definition. If a future widget feature needs a direct definition read,
it adds a SCOPED grant then -- a new decision with its own evidence.

@lookup:MJ: Row Level Security Filters.Name=MJ Forms: Respondent Own Distribution

_comments: Read on the form itself. The automation runtime loads the Form to dispatch against its published snapshot, so without this EVERY automation fails on a fresh install with 'Does NOT have permission to Read MJ_BizApps_Forms: Forms records' -- the response is saved and every side effect is skipped. Found by smoke:binding the first time the shipped role was used instead of one the smoke fixture had over-granted.

Read on questions. loadFormResponseContext resolves each answer's question type from here; without it every answer degrades to questionType 'ShortText' with an empty prompt, which no consumer can distinguish from a form genuinely built that way.
Shipped by V202608241700__v0.11.x__Automation_Runner_AI_Prompt_Run_Write.sql under this
SAME id, so a regenerated seed reproduces this row rather than minting a duplicate under a
fresh GUID -- __mj.EntityPermission has no unique constraint on (EntityID, RoleID), so a
duplicate is silently additive and unions into the effective permission.
Read + Create + Update, NO Delete. MJ's prompt engine inserts an AI Prompt Run when a run
starts and updates it on completion; it never deletes one. Delete is withheld because a
runner that can remove prompt-run rows can erase the record of its own executions -- the
same reasoning that keeps CanCreate off the Form Uploads ledger grant above.
This was the first grant here on a CORE __mj entity; the Action Execution Logs record
below is the second. The prompt-run ledger is where MJ records that an AI call happened at
all, so any principal permitted to run a prompt must be able to write it; 'Integration' and
'Widget Guest', the other non-interactive roles, hold the same grant on this entity already.
Shipped by V202608242100__v0.11.x__Automation_Runner_Person_Write.sql under this SAME id, so
a regenerated seed reproduces this row rather than minting a duplicate under a fresh GUID.
'Forms: Upsert Respondent Person' exists to match-or-create one of these and stamp
FormResponse.RespondentPersonID with the result, and 'Forms: Bind Response To Entity' writes
the same table. Neither could, on any host where an operator had not hand-inserted this row
-- which is how #60 found it: the grant was live in a dev database under an id that appeared
in no migration and no metadata file, the signature of a fix applied and never shipped.
Read + Create + Update, NO Delete. Read for the match-by-email that prevents duplicate
People (#47), Create for a first-time respondent, Update because entity binding merges into
a matched record rather than only creating. Delete is withheld: nothing on this path removes
a Person, and a runner that could would let an anonymous submission destroy a subject record.
This entity belongs to bizapps-common, not to Forms. Forms declares that app as a HARD
dependency in mj-app.json precisely so it can build on it with real foreign keys, and
FormResponse.RespondentPersonID is one of them -- so a principal Forms invents, to run an
action Forms ships, against a table Forms already points at, is Forms' grant to make.
Shipped by V202608242110__v0.11.x__Automation_Runner_Action_Execution_Log_Write.sql under
this SAME id, so a regenerated seed reproduces this row rather than minting a duplicate.
MJ's action engine writes one of these per execution -- inserted at start, updated at
completion. Without the grant the automation still RUNS and FormAutomationRun is still
written, so this cost the audit trail rather than the work. It also left a column Forms
ships permanently null: FormAutomationRun.ActionExecutionLogID is a foreign key to this
entity, and on the database where #60 was found all 134 automation runs carried NULL there,
successes included. Forms' own ledger could not be joined to MJ's.
Read + Create + Update, NO Delete -- exactly what 'Developer' holds on this entity.
'Integration' additionally holds Delete, which a runner has no reason to and which would let
it erase the evidence of its own executions.
